item.title: SABSing Is a New College Dating Trend
item.description:
Mating

SABSing Is a New College Dating Trend

The SABS approach, though a new college trend, is not new or restricted to colleges.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • SABS stands for "see and be seen." SABSing is about hanging out in a public area and being approachable.
  • The term is new but this more open approach has long been common in various countries and cultures.
  • It may reflect a broader interest in more authentic and IRL connections that are less planned/transactional.
  • SABSing can bring more serendipity into your life. Just be reasonably vigilant, and know how to be direct.

If you are on a college campus, maybe you see a new trend. It's students wanting to "see and be seen" more or SABS for short. And as you'll soon see, SABSing is about hanging out in a public place and making yourself more visible and approachable in order to attract more spontaneous connections for dating, friendship, or otherwise. You'll see how SABSing doesn't have to be limited to college campuses, either.

How to Do SABSing

To do the SABSing thing, first go to some highly-trafficked public area—such as a park, a campus lawn, a popular coffee shop, a busy thoroughfare, the entrance to your promiscuous friend's domicile, or wherever you are more likely to encounter many random people. Then show via your body language that you are clearly open to off-the-cuff conversations to develop. This means not doing anything that may say, "Don't bother me"—like wearing headphones, staying focused on your oh-so-important smartphone, or staring intensely at your groin. Instead, maintain an open posture and readily establish eye contact, smile at, and say hello to people who may approach you.

SABSing is the opposite of what many may usually do in public settings—which is to try to remain unseen and just stick to the same familiar people. It's also the opposite of what you may do when you are busy—namely, always having a clear plan and not simply lingering somewhere. SABSing is more about taking in your surroundings and the moment while embracing serendipity and the possibility that a chance encounter may lead to something unexpectedly wonderful.

Where Did SABSing Originate?

Now, it's not easy to see where and when this specific SABSing term originated. In a piece in 34th Street, a magazine that's run by University of Pennsylvania students, the magazine's editor–in–chief Natalia Castillo indicated that it's "unknown" when the term first got established. Her piece did help readers see how established on college campuses SABSing has already become, though, when she wrote, "SABSing is an art—you duck for cover when you see that ex you swore you never wanted to see again, but you eagerly try to make eye contact with your class crush as you cross paths on Locust for the fifth time in a week." She also mentioned how friendly SABSing can be: "And of course, there's no better exhilarating rush than running into your best friend while SABSing."

Nevertheless, the practice of SABSing has existed long before it got this new SABS term and well beyond college campuses. In many different parts of the world, from various countries in Europe to Asia to Africa to South America, people of all ages have long hung out in public areas in ways more conducive to impromptu conversations. For example, in Italy, there is la passeggiata, which is the custom of leisurely strolling through the center of town in the early evening hours so that you can see your neighbors and connect with the surrounding community.

This is very different from what you may be seeing in many American towns and cities these days, where a lot of public areas remain fairly deserted, and people spend a lot of their time in separate compartments—whether it's in a car, cubicle, or some other cubbyhole. You can live in a place for years without ever getting to know your neighbors. Heck, I've been in workplaces in San Francisco and Pittsburgh where simply strolling to meet someone in the adjoining office can be met with what-do-you-want dagger eyes. Rather than the opportunity for connection, there can be distrust even before any interactions occur.

Why Has SABSing Become a Trend?

There has been a larger trend towards more IRL events—with IRL here standing for "in real life" rather than "Ireland." At the beginning of this year, I covered this IRL trend for Forbes in an article entitled, "Trend Towards IRL Events With More Authenticity. What’s Behind It."

Given this title, your next question may be what's behind the trend. Well, the article listed two big possibilities. One is the ongoing loneliness epidemic that's left people craving more in-person connections. The other is a combination of digital fatigue and backlash against dating apps, social media, and other things that have shifted in-person interactions online.

The interest in SABSing could be a reaction to another sad development as well—many people being very inauthentic and transactional in their interactions. There's so much advice out there on how to present yourself in certain ways, fake-it-till-you-make-it, and only spend time with people who can get you somewhere career- or social status-wise. It certainly doesn't help that social media influencers, politicians, business leaders, and, yes, daters regularly present very heavily curated and thus inauthentic images of themselves.

Plus, these days, college students can be the products of a whole lot of hyperplanning. It's no longer just-see-what-college-you-get-into as it was in years past. Nowadays, many parents and kids seemingly start planning their college applications as soon as they've mastered the whole go in the toilet thing. All of these things can leave a lot of life less open to spontaneity and serendipity.

SABSing Can Be Very Positive With Some Cautions

Perhaps this SABSing thing is an expected SABS-lash against various longstanding trends that have long needed correcting. It's hard to argue against SABSing and openly say, "Don't be open. Don't be open about meeting new people." Why not be open rather than close yourself off to the interesting, unexpected opportunities that life may have to offer? And regardless of your age, you could learn from what's happening in colleges and do some SABSing yourself.

At the same time, though, it's good to remain reasonably vigilant. Castillo did warn, for example, about maybe avoiding the ex that you don't want to see. And there is always the possibility of some creeps creeping into your space.

Moreover, being open does mean knowing when to close off the conversation. Maybe it's after one too many lines like, "Well, here I am. What are your other two wishes?" or when the person has demonstrated that he or she does not respect boundaries. That's when SABSing goes beyond simply "see and be seen" and includes some direct "now see here" communications to tell certain people that you don't want to see them any longer.

All that being said, for all the sad trends out there, the SABS thing can be a good way to go. Let's see what else it may bring.

item.title: Beyond the "Good Match": Mental Health Stigma in South Asian Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

Beyond the "Good Match": Mental Health Stigma in South Asian Relationships

The hidden impact of mental health stigma on South Asian relationships

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Disclosing mental health concerns is a personal choice, but can be challenging for South Asians.
  • Navigating relationship challenges is seldom discussed in South Asian families.
  • There is a fear of being discriminated for a mental health issue by a partner and their family.

This post is part 1 of a series.

Growing up, I frequently overheard whispered conversations about relationship struggles in my South Asian community. Often, the stories involved young men discovering after marriage that their wife had an undisclosed mental health condition.

Typically, families would react with shock, saying, "Had we known the girl had these issues, we never would have let that marriage happen." Rarely was their concern about what she might have been experiencing. Instead, the focus was: "The poor husband, he's such a good guy. What bad karma."

Occasionally, I would hear about a husband’s struggles—again, he would receive sympathy, but the concerns usually centered on the impact to his career rather than his mental health, i.e. being laid off or having to take time off. Meanwhile, many of the affected women quietly become the emotional breadwinners of the family, juggling work, children, and a partner who refused to seek help.

"It was only after my husband began experiencing paranoia at work and had to go to doctor that I found out they have a history of schizophrenia in the family. His family is very hush hush about it, obviously; it's not something people share. Still, I wish I had known that this was a possibility." —Rani, 35

Disclosing mental health concerns is a personal choice, but it can be especially challenging within the South Asian community. While physical illness is more openly discussed, mental health remains highly stigmatized, reinforcing messages to "stay away from alliances with those who are emotionally weak."

Unfortunately, “Many people grow up with deeply judgmental beliefs about mental health, mental illness, therapy, and even the idea of needing support," says Tanya Mitra, certified life coach and founder of The REMIXED Relationship. "In my experience, many of the people who hold those beliefs may have benefited from support themselves but were never taught to recognize it or see seeking help as an option.”

In the case of Rani and many others, the complexity lies in the fact that her husband’s family didn’t share about their mental health history for fear of being discriminated against as an alliance. But on the other hand, silence on the issue made Rani feel blind-sided. Yet the greater challenge isn't choosing a partner with mental health concerns, it’s when those concerns remain hidden, untreated, or unspoken about within the relationship.

Imagination vs. Reality in South Asian Relationships

"She was fine until she wasn't. I don't know what happened. She's angry and tearful all the time. She used to be full of life and fun. I wish we could go back to that." —Rajiv, 28

"We are taught (thanks Bollywood!) that love and romance is exciting, fun, and bring out the best in us," says Ankur Varma, psychotherapist and founder of BrownManTherapy. While Indian cinema often sets unrealistic expectations for romance, Varma notes that "building a long-term relationship is about weathering storms, the ebbs and flows of the relationship as well as the human with whom we're partnering. This means that we need to share our challenges and learn ways of supporting each other. Sometimes stigma means that there isn't space to share these things."

Yet many South Asians are never taught how to have these conversations.

Navigating relationships is seldom discussed in South Asian families, where parents often choose to show rather than tell. In previous generations, advice was usually tailored around narrow gender-specific behaviors. Girls were often taught not to complain, while boys were taught to be strong and stoic for the family. There were few dialogues on how to assert yourself, share emotions, deal with sex, or be vulnerable. These topics were either ignored, frowned upon, or seen as indulgent.

While these patterns are changing, some scripts remain untouched. Conversations about how mental health may affect a future marriage are even rarer. As Varma explains: “I think culturally, we believe that marriage is a mandatory step in life, and it's an indicator of success. When we frame it that way, we sometimes skip over the actual relationship building that is necessary to long-term relational success, things like communication, support, resilience, etc."

Too often, this one-dimensional view of marriage overlooks the emotional skills needed to sustain a healthy partnership. Often times, an amorphous idea of “love” is used as an antidote to all problems as well as a reason not to share deeper issues. Varma astutely states that due to love and “the pressure to get married, we tend to hide away some of the negatives or avoid the harder conversations, which can really come back to bite us.”

The line of questioning parents have about potential partners (which often serve as fodder for humor among the diaspora) are indeed problematic. Questions regarding achievement and education, career choice, and family background are often posed in judgmental terms (i.e. do they have a “good” job are they from a “good’ family, etc.). These could be posed with more nuance, as well as the introduction of deeper and more meaningful questions: How do they handle stress? Or communicate difficult emotions? What is their willingness to seek help? These questions may ultimately matter far more than whether someone has experienced depression, anxiety, or other mental health challenges.

Looking Ahead: Supporting Each Other for the Long Haul

So, what happens when the honeymoon phase or wedding is over and real life/marriage begins? Once two lives become intertwined, struggles that were once private become relational. This is where the conversation must shift, from whether someone has mental health challenges to how couples navigate them together.

Stay tuned for Part 2: "When Love Becomes Caregiving"

item.title: Therapeutic Flexibility is Important in Clinical Hypnosis
item.description:
Hypnosis

Therapeutic Flexibility is Important in Clinical Hypnosis

How rapport can be enhanced between clinicians and their patients.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Utilization involves applying a patient’s interests within the therapeutic process.
  • Play therapy allows the clinician to follows a child’s lead while they are playing.
  • Characters and events within videogames can serve as hypnotic metaphors.
Source: Pixel-shot/Shutterstock

When I recently led a consultation group about the use of clinical hypnosis, one of the participants, a Gen X counselor of children and adolescents who is new to hypnosis, confessed that she had little knowledge of the videogames played by her patients such as Minecraft, Roblox, and Fortnite.

Thus, when she has taught them how to employ imagery to calm themselves, she has suggested using images that she herself has found to be calming including scenes from the beach, mountains, or forests.

I reminded the consultation group of Milton Erickson’s concept of utilization (1959), which can be defined broadly as applying an individual patient’s interests, experiences, and response patterns within the therapeutic process.

Such an approach enhances rapport between clinicians and their patients because their interactions occur in a world that is familiar and comfortable to the patients.

Thus, the effectiveness of their therapy is enhanced, as opposed to offering a technique with which a clinician might be comfortable but is of little relevance to a patient.

I suggested that the counselor ask her patients to show her how their videogames work, and that she can offer therapeutic suggestions as she is shown these games. This would be a form of play therapy in which the clinician follows the child’s lead while they are playing (Ray et al., 2015).

In this way, the patient can express their feelings and develop coping skills while playing a game (Zayeni et al., 2020). Further, I suggested that the counselor can use characters and events within the videogames to serve as metaphors as part of her work with hypnosis.

Grizzy and the Lemmings

As an example, I described a 7-year-old boy with whom I have been working recently, who has difficulty controlling his anger and frustrations,.

His mother told me that his favorite videos involve Grizzy and the Lemmings. She said that she strongly dislikes these shows because they contain no dialogue, and she felt they have no redeeming value.

I had never heard of this cartoon video series, but I expressed interest in watching one of the episodes because it was of great interest to my patient. I pulled one up through You Tube on my computer, and started the six-minute video.

In this particular episode, Grizzy, a grizzly bear, is resting in a cabin and is tormented by lemmings, which appear to be small mammals that reminded me of the more famous minions from Despicable Me fame. The characters only spoke gibberish.

My patient stood transfixed next to me watching the episode. I recognized that in my lingo he was trance-fixed. This meant that he had entered a hypnotic state spontaneously, in which he would be more receptive to my suggestions than in his usual state of awareness.

In the cartoon, Grizzy became very angry at the lemmings’ behavior and started blowing his top. At that point I paused the video and asked my patient, “Can you think of anything Grizzy could do besides explode in anger?”

We discussed various possibilities including calling his mother, taking some deep breaths, or leaving the cabin to take a walk in nature. Of course, these suggestions all related to my patient’s work on regulating his own emotions.

I restarted the video. The lemmings had mercifully left the cabin at that point, no doubt planning more shenanigans. Meanwhile, Grizzy started meditating and taking slow deep breaths.

Again, I paused the video and asked my patient what he thought of the idea of taking slow deep breaths to calm himself.

I reviewed box breathing with him at that time: inhaling slowly for a count of four, holding his breath for a count of four, exhaling for a count of four, and again holding his breath for a count of four.

We ended up watching only two minutes of the show, but I managed to utilize my patient’s intense interest in the cartoon to make important therapeutic suggestions.

I encouraged his mother to consider similarly watching cartoons with him to discuss what he might learn from them. In this way she likely will enhance her ability to educate her son.

Takeaway

Health care providers who first learn to do hypnosis often express their insecurity because of their inexperience with this therapeutic approach. Thus, they sometimes want to follow a “script” containing therapeutic suggestions that can be read or told to a patient.

However, a script usually does not reflect a patient’s interests, and sticking to a script prevents therapeutic adjustments. Therefore, I encourage providers to remain flexible in their approach and to learn how to therapeutically utilize whatever comes up during interactions with their patients.
